title: Voice model capture script
notes: Use one stable lossless mono recording setup for every prompt. Keep immutable master takes, a take ledger, and exact transcript alignment outside Git.

The three tiers organize recording order and coverage; they do not promise a particular result. Record the complete 156-prompt programme when possible and judge reference suitability through the private review passes.

Block B passages are ORIGINAL writing, deliberately. Harry Potter and Lord of the Rings are both in copyright, so they are not reproduced here; instead these passages are written in the same epic and dramatic register, which has the practical advantage that each one is tuned to hit a specific emotion at a specific duration. Block I is genuine public-domain literature for the same purpose.

Add authorised public material by extending this canonical JSON with an explicit item ID, style, direction, source, and transcript. Do not rely on undocumented commands or filename-only emotion labels.

Read each prompt naturally and follow its situation rather than forcing a vocal manoeuvre. Compare candidate references through the private blinded-listening workflow and keep every outcome outside this public pack.

narration_neutral.label: Neutral narration
narration_neutral.direction: Even pace, clear, unhurried. Explaining something to a competent colleague. No performance, no smile-voice. This is the workhorse and most demo audio will use it.

warm_friendly.label: Warm and friendly
warm_friendly.direction: Smile naturally while you read. Keep the delivery friendly, slightly slower, slightly lower, with softer breath. Greeting someone you like.

excited_energetic.label: Excited and energetic
excited_energetic.direction: Genuine enthusiasm, not shouting. Faster, brighter, more pitch movement. Lean forward. Showing someone the thing you are proud of. Keep articulation crisp.

serious_authoritative.label: Serious and authoritative
serious_authoritative.direction: Lower, slower, weightier. Longer pauses. Land on the full stops. Telling someone something that carries consequence. Authority through calm, not force.

curious_questioning.label: Curious and questioning
curious_questioning.direction: Genuine inquiry, thinking aloud. Let questions actually rise at the end. Never read a question as a statement.

empathetic_calm.label: Empathetic and calm
empathetic_calm.direction: Soft, unhurried, low energy but fully engaged. Quieter than neutral but stay voiced; do not go breathy or whispery. Reassuring someone frustrated.

emphatic_punchy.label: Emphatic and punchy
emphatic_punchy.direction: Short sentences, hard stress, real silence between them. Let each full stop breathe about half a second. Deliberate and confident.

awe_wonder.label: Awe and wonder
awe_wonder.direction: Tell someone plainly about something that genuinely impressed you. Do not sustain the vowels, slow down, go breathy, or become reverent. Keep your ordinary pace and let the words carry the wonder.

sorrow_grief.label: Sorrow and grief
sorrow_grief.direction: Low, slow, slightly unsupported at the ends of phrases, as if the breath is running out. Do not sob or crack deliberately; restrained grief reads as far more real than performed grief.

anger_fierce.label: Anger, fierce
anger_fierce.direction: Hard consonants, forward placement, tight throat. Controlled fury rather than yelling: pushed volume clips the mic and reads as thin, whereas clenched intensity reads as dangerous.

tender_intimate.label: Tender and intimate
tender_intimate.direction: Close, soft, warm, almost confiding. Slower and quieter than empathetic, with more air, as though the listener is right beside you and nobody else can hear.

suspense_hushed.label: Suspense, hushed
suspense_hushed.direction: Quiet, tight, urgent. Use short breaths and a voiced whisper rather than a true whisper so every word remains clear. Put the tension in the jaw, not the volume.

playful_wry.label: Playful and wry
playful_wry.direction: Dry, amused, faintly arch. Let the timing carry the joke rather than the volume. Underplay the punchline; a wry line sold too hard stops being wry.

triumphant_declaratory.label: Triumphant and declaratory
triumphant_declaratory.direction: Pleased and generous - relief and satisfaction rather than a proclamation. Keep the vowels natural and do not project as if speaking to a hall. Think of telling your team it finally shipped.

items.note: SILENCE. Do not speak, do not move, do not touch the desk. This measures the room noise floor, which sets the quality ceiling for everything after it.
items.text: [record 12 seconds of complete silence]

items.note: Normal speaking volume, the level you would actually narrate at. Peak level and SNR are checked before you commit to the real script.
items.text: This is a level check at my normal narration volume. One, two, three, four, five. The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog. I am speaking exactly as I would for a real demo recording.

items.note: Now your LOUDEST likely moment, so headroom can be confirmed and nothing clips later in Block B.
items.text: And here is the best part! Look at that! Fourteen thousand rows, instantly!

items.note: One continuous take. Do not let the energy fall on the last sentence.
items.text: The dashboard pulls live data from three separate sources and reconciles them every fifteen seconds. On the left you can see the current queue depth. On the right, the same figures broken out by region, so you can tell at a glance where the backlog is forming.

items.note: Steady, procedural. Slight downward inflection on each full stop.
items.text: Setting this up takes two steps. First, you connect your data source, and the system reads the schema automatically. Second, you pick the fields you actually care about. Everything else stays hidden until you need it, which keeps the default view readable.

items.note: Same voice as the previous two. Consistency across the three takes is what makes this style reliable.
items.text: Underneath, each request is logged with a timestamp, the user who made it, and the result. That history is what makes the audit trail possible. You can filter it by date, export it as a spreadsheet, or hand it straight to your compliance team.

items.note: Actually smile. Keep the smile all the way to the final word.
items.text: Hey, thanks for stopping by. I want to walk you through something we have been building for a few months now, and honestly, I am quite proud of how it turned out. It is going to take about four minutes, so grab a coffee and settle in.

items.note: A sign-off. Warm, relaxed, slightly slower than neutral.
items.text: So that is the whole tour. I hope it gave you a decent feel for how it works day to day. If anything looked interesting, or if you just want to poke around yourself, the link is right below this video. Thanks for watching.

items.note: Inclusive and welcoming.
items.text: Before we dive in, a quick word about who this is for. If you have ever had to pull a report together on a Friday evening, you are exactly the person we built this for. Welcome, you are in good company.

items.note: Bright and fast, but keep articulation crisp. Excitement, not volume.
items.text: Okay, this is the part I have been waiting to show you. Watch what happens when I hit refresh. That entire report, every chart, every number, rebuilt in under two seconds. The first time I saw that, I actually laughed out loud.

items.note: Building energy across the sentences. Do not plateau early.
items.text: And here is the best bit. You do not have to configure any of it. It just works, straight out of the box, on day one. No setup call, no onboarding form, no waiting around for someone to provision your account.

items.note: Hit the standalone exclamation properly. That single word carries the style.
items.text: Look at that. Fourteen thousand rows, sorted, filtered, and grouped, instantly. This used to take our analysts an entire afternoon. An afternoon! Now it happens faster than you can finish reading the question. That is the whole point of this thing.

items.note: Drop your pitch. Slow down. Let the last sentence land hard and cold.
items.text: Let us be clear about the stakes. A single misconfigured permission can expose customer records to the entire organisation. It has happened to companies far larger than ours, and it will happen again. This is not a theoretical risk. It is a Tuesday afternoon.

items.note: Measured and factual. Authority through calm, not force.
items.text: Every credential is encrypted at rest and in transit. Nothing is written to disk in plain text. Access is logged, reviewed monthly, and revoked the moment someone changes role. These are not optional extras. They are the minimum bar for handling data like this.

items.note: Grave and direct. Slight weight on the repeated word at the end.
items.text: The current process has three failure points, and we have hit all three in the past year. Each time, the cost was measured in days of lost work. We cannot keep absorbing that. Something has to change, and it has to change now.

items.note: Let the two questions genuinely rise, then answer yourself thoughtfully.
items.text: So what actually happens when two people edit the same record at once? Does one of them silently lose their work? Or does the system notice, stop, and ask? That question sounds small, but it decides whether anyone trusts the tool.

items.note: The numbered guesses should sound like real guesses, each with its own rise.
items.text: Why does this matter? Well, think about how you work now. How many browser tabs do you have open just to answer one question? Three? Five? And how many of them are showing numbers that disagree with each other?

items.note: Open on a real question, then narrow into the answer.
items.text: But is it fast enough to use in a live meeting? That was the real test. Not fast in a benchmark, not fast on a developer's laptop, but fast while eleven people are watching and waiting for an answer.

items.note: Soft and slow. Quieter than neutral, but keep it voiced. Do not go breathy.
items.text: I know this part is frustrating. You have done everything right, the file is correct, and it still will not upload. We have all been there, staring at a progress bar at half past six. So let me show you what is actually going wrong, and how to fix it.

items.note: Reassuring and patient. Imagine talking to a nervous new colleague.
items.text: It is completely normal to feel a bit lost the first week. There is a lot here, and nobody expects you to hold it all in your head. Take it slowly. You only need three of these screens to do your job well.

items.note: A genuine apology, then gentle resolve. Sincere, not performed.
items.text: If you have lost work this way before, I am sorry. It is a genuinely awful feeling, and it was not your fault. The old system made it far too easy to do. That is precisely why we changed it. You should not have to be careful for the software's sake.

items.note: Real silence between the short sentences, roughly half a second each. Do not rush them together.
items.text: One dashboard. One number. One source of truth. No spreadsheets. No arguing about whose figures are right. You open it, you look, you know. That is it. That is the whole pitch.

items.note: Three isolated words to open. Stress each equally, with a beat between.
items.text: Faster. Simpler. Cheaper. Pick all three, because for once you actually can. Ninety seconds to set up. Zero training required. And it costs less than the tool you are already unhappy with.

items.note: Imperative and direct. The final one-word sentence needs a full beat before it.
items.text: Stop guessing. Start measuring. The data is already there, sitting in your systems, waiting. All you have to do is look at it. So look at it. Today.

items.note: Slower than feels natural. Let the vowels open and sustain. You are seeing something you cannot quite believe.
items.text: And then the mist drew back, and he saw it at last. Towers of white stone rising sheer from the valley floor, catching the first light, higher than any work of mortal hands. Seven walls, seven gates, and above them all a banner he had only ever heard named in songs.

items.note: Hushed reverence rather than volume. The last clause should feel like a discovery.
items.text: The doors were older than the kingdom. Carved into them were the names of every soul who had passed through, and there were more names than there are stars a man can count on a clear night. She set her palm against the wood, and felt it answer her, warm as a living thing.

items.note: Let the silence after the third sentence do the work before you finish.
items.text: Below them the whole world opened. Rivers like threads of silver, forests dark as spilled ink, and beyond it all the sea, burning gold from edge to edge. Nobody spoke. There was nothing to say that would not have made it smaller.

items.note: Restrained. Let the breath run a little short at the ends of phrases. Do not perform crying.
items.text: They buried him at dusk, under the ash tree he had planted as a boy. There was no speech, because nobody could manage one. His sister put her hand on the stone and left it there a long while, and when she finally walked away, she did not look back.

items.note: Quiet and inward, as if talking mostly to yourself.
items.text: I keep finding his things. A glove in the pocket of my coat. A book with the page still turned down where he stopped reading. Every one of them is a small door I cannot help opening, and behind every one of them, he is still alive.

items.note: Flat and tired for most of it, then a small break of feeling on the last two words.
items.text: She was the last of them. She had outlived her brothers, her husband, and both of her children, and when the letters stopped coming there was no one left who remembered her name as a girl. That is the part nobody warns you about. Not the dying. The forgetting.

items.note: Clenched, not shouted. Watch the level meter: pushed volume will clip and clipping ruins the clip permanently.
items.text: No. You do not get to say that to me. Not after everything I gave to this, not after the years I spent holding it together while you looked the other way. You will sit down, and you will listen, and for once in your life you will hear it.

items.note: Open on a hard stop, then hold the fury level rather than escalating into a shout.
items.text: Enough! I have heard enough. You came into my house, you ate at my table, and you lied to my face about the one thing that mattered. Get out. Take your horse and your gold and your excuses, and do not come back while I am still breathing.

items.note: Cold anger rather than hot. Quieter, and more frightening for it.
items.text: They burned the village. Not the soldiers, not the enemy, but our own men, on our own orders, because someone in a warm room decided it was simpler. I will carry that. But I will not forgive it, and I will not pretend it was necessary.

items.note: Very close and soft, but stay voiced. Slow the whole thing down by about a quarter.
items.text: Hey. You are alright. I have got you. Just breathe with me, in and out, that is it. Nothing has to be decided tonight, and nobody is angry with you, and you are not in trouble. Whatever it is, we will look at it together in the morning.

items.note: Fond and amused and a little wistful, all at once.
items.text: You were so small. I could hold all of you in my two hands, and I was terrified I would do it wrong. And now look at you. Taller than me, arguing with me, wonderfully certain about everything. I would not change a single day of it.

items.note: Almost nothing in the voice. Warm, low, unhurried, content.
items.text: Stay a minute longer. The fire is still good and the roads will keep. I like the quiet with you in it. That is all. There is nothing I need to say, I would just rather you were here than not.

items.note: Voiced whisper, urgent, short breaths. Keep the vocal folds engaged so every word remains clearly voiced.
items.text: Do not move. Listen. There it is again, under the floor, the same three taps, and it has been an hour since anyone else was in this house. I locked the door myself. I checked it twice. Whatever is down there, it knows we are standing here.

items.note: Tight and fast and low. Instructions given under real pressure.
items.text: Keep your voice down and keep walking. Do not look at the man by the fountain and do not slow down when we pass him. If we reach the bridge before the bell rings we will be fine. If we do not, then you run, and you do not stop for me.

items.note: Dread rather than fear. Slow, deliberate, and quiet right to the final word.
items.text: The lamp went out on its own. There was no draught, the window was shut, and the wick was hardly touched. And in the dark, for just a moment, I heard something breathing that was not either of us.

items.note: Dry and arch. Underplay it. The timing carries the joke, not the volume.
items.text: Oh, marvellous. Another meeting about the meeting. I shall bring a cushion and my will. Honestly, at this point I have spent more of my life in that room than in my own house, and the room has better coffee, which is the truly insulting part.

items.note: Deadpan the whole way, and leave a real beat before the last sentence.
items.text: He assured me, with a completely straight face, that he had read the whole document. All ninety pages. In eleven minutes. Between two other calls. I said nothing. I simply asked him what he thought of appendix four. There is no appendix four.

items.note: Mock-formal innocence. Enjoy it, but do not wink at the audience.
items.text: I am not saying I told you so. I would never say that. I am simply noting, for the historical record, that a certain person predicted this exact outcome in March, in writing, and was described at the time as being unhelpfully negative.

items.note: Chest-forward and ringing. Proclaiming to a room. Full breath, strong finals.
items.text: It held. The wall held, the gate held, and when the sun came up there were still men standing on it. Sound the bells. Every one of them, all the way to the coast, until the last village knows. Tonight we are still here, and tomorrow we are still here.

items.note: Formal proclamation. Slower and grander than feels comfortable.
items.text: Then let it be written, and let it be read aloud in every hall from the mountains to the sea. The debt is paid. The exile is ended. From this day forward no one bearing that name shall be turned from any door in this kingdom.

items.note: Modern and warm rather than grand. Exhausted, delighted triumph.
items.text: We did it. Eleven months, four false starts, and one very long weekend, and it is done, and it works. Look at the board. Every single light is green. Go home. Sleep. And then come back, because I have got an idea about the next one.

items.text: Let me show you what a normal Monday looks like now. You open the dashboard, and the first thing you see is the one number that actually matters. How many orders are stuck. Last Monday it was six. This Monday it is zero, and that is not luck, it is the new validation step catching problems before they reach the queue. If you click through, you get the detail. Who submitted it, what failed, and the exact field that caused it. No more guessing, no more digging through logs at seven in the morning. And here is the part I like most. When something does go wrong, the person who can fix it gets a message immediately, with the record attached. They do not have to come looking for it. In the four weeks since we turned this on, average resolution time has gone from about eleven hours to just under forty minutes. Same team, same volume, same systems underneath. We just stopped losing information between the steps.

items.note: One take. Starts grave, softens in the middle where you say you want to be honest, then resolves steady and factual. Let that arc happen naturally.
items.text: For years, the reconciliation ran overnight, and nobody looked at it until morning. If it failed at two in the morning, you found out at nine, and by then the day was already lost. That happened eleven times last year. Eleven mornings where the first thing somebody did was apologise to a customer for a number that was wrong. I want to be honest. That was not a technology problem. The code worked. The problem was that no human being was told. So we changed the one thing that mattered. Now, if reconciliation fails, three people get woken up, and the system holds the bad figures back instead of publishing them. It sounds almost too simple to matter. But since March, we have had two failures, both caught within four minutes, and neither one reached a customer. Nobody had to apologise for anything. That is the whole improvement. Not smarter code. Just information reaching a person in time to act on it.

items.note: One take. Pure instructional walkthrough. Steady, patient, slightly slower than conversational. This is the exact register most demo narration needs.
items.text: Let us walk through setting up your first workspace. Start by clicking New Workspace in the top right corner. Give it a name you will recognise in six months, because you will not remember what Test Two meant. Next, choose a data source. If your source is not listed, pick Generic SQL and paste the connection string. The system will read the schema and show you every table it found, along with a row count, so you can sanity check that you are pointed at production and not at a stale copy. Now select the tables you need. My advice is to start with fewer than you think. You can always add more, and a smaller workspace loads faster. Once you have chosen, click Validate. This takes about twenty seconds, and it checks three things. That the credentials work, that the tables are readable, and that nothing has a column type we cannot map. If all three pass, you are done. Click Create, and your workspace opens automatically.

items.note: One take, dramatic register, with a real emotional arc: wonder, then dread, then resolve. Keep the movement natural rather than holding one mood.
items.text: They came over the last ridge a little before dawn, and none of them spoke, because the valley below was not what the maps had promised. Where there should have been forest there was a lake, black and perfectly still, and standing in the middle of it, half sunk and leaning, was a tower of pale stone. It was enormous. It was older than anything any of them had a word for. Birds went around it rather than over it. And then the light came up properly, and they saw that the whole surface of the lake was covered in small boats, hundreds of them, empty, drifting, all facing the tower as though they had been rowed out and abandoned there on purpose. Nobody wanted to be the first to say it. Finally the youngest of them, who had never been further than the market road, put down her pack and said, well. We did come all this way. And she started down the slope, and one by one, so did everyone else.

items.text: To be, or not to be, that is the question: whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, or to take arms against a sea of troubles, and by opposing end them.

items.text: Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow, creeps in this petty pace from day to day, to the last syllable of recorded time; and all our yesterdays have lighted fools the way to dusty death. Out, out, brief candle!

items.text: Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary, over many a quaint and curious volume of forgotten lore, while I nodded, nearly napping, suddenly there came a tapping, as of someone gently rapping, rapping at my chamber door.

items.text: Call me Ishmael. Some years ago, never mind how long precisely, having little or no money in my purse, and nothing particular to interest me on shore, I thought I would sail about a little and see the watery part of the world.

items.source: public domain: Charlotte Bronte, Jane Eyre, 1847
items.note: Rising defiance. Starts contained and controlled, ends unmistakably free. Do not shout the last line; let it ring.
items.text: Do you think, because I am poor, obscure, plain, and little, I am soulless and heartless? You think wrong! I have as much soul as you, and full as much heart. I am no bird; and no net ensnares me: I am a free human being with an independent will.

items.note: Measured and steady, one condition at a time. Resist building to a climax; the restraint is the point.
items.text: If you can keep your head when all about you are losing theirs and blaming it on you; if you can trust yourself when all men doubt you, but make allowance for their doubting too; if you can wait and not be tired by waiting.

items.text: I should probably explain how I ended up doing this for a living. It was not a plan. I finished university with a degree I had no intention of using, took a job that was meant to last three months, and stayed for six years. Somewhere in the middle of that I discovered I was quite good at explaining complicated things to people who were in a hurry.

items.text: Most systems do not fail all at once. They fail slowly, in ways nobody notices, until one ordinary Tuesday the thing that has been quietly broken for months finally matters. The interesting question is never why it broke. It is why nobody saw it, and the answer is almost always that the information existed but never reached a person who could act on it.

items.text: The office had one window that actually opened, and by unspoken agreement it belonged to whoever arrived first. I was rarely first. What I remember most from that year is not the work but the sound of the building waking up. The lift, the kettle, somebody's terrible radio two floors down, and then the particular silence that arrived about ten minutes before a deadline.

items.text: There is a useful distinction between a problem and a constraint. A problem is something you can solve, and once solved it stays solved. A constraint is something you design around, and it never goes away. Most of the frustration I see in teams comes from treating a constraint as though it were a problem, and then being surprised when the effort produces nothing durable.

items.text: People ask me what the hardest part is, and they expect me to say something technical. It is not technical. The hardest part is getting eleven people who all agree in principle to also agree on the specific words in a specific document by a specific Friday. Everything else is comparatively straightforward.

An old bridge, closed for years, still carried a faded sign warning lorries about a weight limit that no longer applied to anything.

items.text: We actually did it. Eleven months, four false starts, and one weekend I would rather not discuss, and it is done, and it works. Look at the board. Every light is green. Go home, sleep, and do not answer your email until Monday.

items.note: One continuous take, plain reading throughout. If you stumble, keep going rather than restarting. Long plain reads yield several candidate windows from one recording, so this is the best value per minute in the whole top-up.
items.text: I have been trying to work out when exactly the job changed, and I think it was the summer we moved buildings. Before that, everything happened in one room. If you needed to know something you turned around and asked, and if the person was not there you waited until they were. It was inefficient in every way that matters on paper, and it worked extremely well. Then we moved, and the team was split across two floors, and something quietly broke that took us a year to notice. Nobody stopped talking to each other. But the conversations became scheduled rather than accidental, and the accidental ones turned out to be the important ones. The problem someone mentions while waiting for the kettle is a different class of problem from the one they put on an agenda. What we lost was not communication. We had more of that than ever, most of it written down, most of it searchable. What we lost was the overhearing. You used to absorb half of what you needed to know without anyone deciding to tell you. I do not think there is a tool that fixes this, which is an awkward thing to believe in my line of work. The closest we have managed is a deliberate habit of saying things out loud that we would previously have said by accident, which sounds trivial and has been surprisingly hard to sustain.

items.note: One continuous take, plain instructional reading at a normal pace. This is the exact register most of your demo narration will need, so it is the most directly useful recording in the top-up.
items.text: Let me walk you through the whole setup, start to finish, at a normal pace. You begin on the workspaces screen. Click New in the top right. Give it a name you will still recognise in six months, which in practice means not calling it Test. The system will ask for a data source next, and this is the only part where you need somebody else's help, because you will need a connection string and most people do not have one to hand. Paste it in and click Check. This takes about twenty seconds. What it is doing is confirming three separate things. That the credentials work, that the tables you asked for are actually readable, and that nothing has a column type we cannot map onto our own. If any of those fail you get a specific message rather than a generic one, which I insisted on, because a generic connection error costs about half a day. Assuming all three pass, you will see a list of every table it found with a row count beside each. Sanity check that. If a table you expect to be enormous shows eleven rows, you are pointed at a stale copy, and it is much better to find that out now. Then choose the tables you actually need. Start with fewer than you think. You can always add more, and a smaller workspace opens faster every single time you use it.
